svg.text: Figure 5.2. Incrementing PTR and HIST: read on port A, write back on port B one cycle later
v1.0 (spec/machine-spec.md §4.9, §4.10) — PTR on the left, HIST on the right
PTR — the write engine's landing pointers
req, and idx = src (modes 2, 4) or the
• req always reads port A and loads the last address register; req(t−1) gives port B to the increment
(address, data, write), otherwise port B is the controller's.
• A controller write that meets an increment is lost. Software sets PTR only between phases (§4.10).
• Port B's read data is unused: the controller never reads PTR.
• Why the eq comp also needs req(t−1): the bypass is only for a write still landing. Without it, a
stale last address (from before the controller set the entry between phases, or junk after reset)
could match, and the mux would take a stale last value.
req, and idx = the histogram digit
• Port B is shared the same way, and the controller's loads read through it too.
• A controller load that meets an increment returns the value the engine wrote, at the engine's
address, not the one asked for. Software reads and clears HIST only between phases (§4.10).
• A count past 17 bits is an error (invariant 6).
• Why the eq comp also needs req(t−1): the bypass is only for a write still landing. Without it, a
stale last address (from before the controller set the entry between phases, or junk after reset)
could match, and the mux would take a stale last value.
IMPORTANT: on a read/write address collision, the write must win.

When idx(t) = last address, port A reads the entry port B is writing in the same cycle. The read data is ignored, so it may be garbage, but the write must land intact. Confirm against the memory compiler's datasheet.
Example: idx 7, 7, 3 arrive on cycles t, t+1, t+2 (k = 2 for PTR, 1 for HIST; req = 0 at t−1)
an increment of PTR[idx] (+2) or HIST[idx] (+1)

junction (lines that cross without a dot don't connect)
Each table does one read-modify-write per cycle: port A reads the entry on cycle t, and port B writes the incremented value back on t+1. Port B is shared
with the controller, and the increment wins. When the same entry is incremented twice in a row, the read result is ignored and the last value is used.
req starts the read and loads the last address register; req(t−1) drives the write.
